extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, scholars, and newspaper professionals (editors/reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of professional standards, legal principles, and educational criteria for American newspaper journalism (early 20th century), centered on the American Society of Newspaper Editors' Canons and related legal/educational rulings. Useful for evaluating newspaper practice, ethics, and journalism curricula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary function of newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary function of newspapers is to communicate to the human race what its members do, feel, and think. Journalism, therefore, demands of its practitioners the widest range of intelligence, of knowledge, and of experience, as well as natural and trained powers of observation and reasoning. To its opportunities as a chronicler are indissolubly linked its obligations as teacher and interpreter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets an overarching standard: journalists must possess broad intelligence, knowledge, experience, observational and reasoning skills; newspapers serve both to chronicle events and to educate/interpret for the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility (ASNE Canon I)
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of a newspaper to attract and hold readers is restricted by nothing but considerations of public welfare. The use of a newspaper makes of the share of public attention it gains serves to determine its sense of responsibility, which it shares with every member of its staff. A journalist who uses his power for any selfish or otherwise unworthy purpose is faithless to a high trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and staff must subordinate commercial or personal gain to the public welfare; possession of audience imposes a duty of responsible conduct across the entire staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of the Press (ASNE Canon II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of the press is to be guarded as a vital right of mankind. It is the unquestionable right to discuss whatever is not explicitly forbidden by law, including the wisdom of any restrictive statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms a broad right to public discussion except where law explicitly forbids; positions protection of critical discussion of statutes as part of press freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence (ASNE Canon III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom from all obligations except that of fidelity to the public interest is vital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subpoints: 1) Promotion of any private interest contrary to the general welfare is incompatible with honest journalism; news from private sources should not be published without public notice of their source or substantiation. 2) Partisanship in editorial comment that knowingly departs from the truth harms journalism; in news columns partisanship is subversive of the profession. (Guides conflicts of interest, source disclosure/substantiation, and limits on partisan distortion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity, Truthfulness, Accuracy (ASNE Canon IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good faith with the reader is the foundation of all journalism worthy of the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subpoints: 1) Newspapers are constrained to be truthful and are not excused for lack of thoroughness or accuracy within their control. 2) Headlines should be fully warranted by the contents of the articles which they surmount. (Directives on diligence, factual accuracy, and headline honesty.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality (ASNE Canon V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound practice makes clear distinction between news reports and expressions of opinion. News reports should be free from opinion or bias of any kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: special articles clearly devoted to advocacy or signed pieces where the author indicates interpretation. (Requires separation of factual reporting from advocacy/opinion; signed advocacy permitted but must be explicit.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair Play (ASNE Canon VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper should not publish unofficial charges affecting reputation or moral character without opportunity given to the accused to be heard; right practice demands the giving of such opportunity in all cases of serious accusation outside judicial proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subpoints: 1) A newspaper should not invade private rights or feelings without sure warrant of public right as distinguished from public curiosity. 2) Newspapers have the privilege and duty to make prompt and complete correction of their own serious mistakes of fact or opinion, whatever their origin. (Guides pre-publication fairness to subjects, restraint on private invasion, and post-publication corrections.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Decency (ASNE Canon VII)
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper cannot escape conviction of insincerity if, while professing high moral purpose, it supplies incentives to base conduct, such as are to be found in details of crime and vice, publication of which is not demonstrably for the general good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Urges newspapers to avoid deliberate pandering to vicious instincts; encourages reliance on public/professional condemnation to check sensationalism when formal enforcement is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter-source confidentiality / reporter's privilege (state law protections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maryland passed a law protecting the confidential communications between a reporter and his source in 1896, and in the thirties seven other states made similar enactments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies a legal protection standard: several states enacted reporter-source confidentiality statutes by the 1930s; relevant to protecting informants and journalists from compelled disclosure in some jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation of news / unfair competition (Associated Press v. International News Service)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 1918 Associated Press vs. the International News Service case, the Court held that the appropriation of news from early bulletins was unfair competition and there was a remedy in a court of equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes a legal standard that copying/appropriating early news bulletins can constitute unfair competition and be remedied by equity; impacts how news agencies and publishers may reuse scoops or bulletins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter compelled to reveal source (criminal-jury context) — limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 1921 case involving Hector Elwell it was ruled that a reporter who reported a grand jury indictment before official announcement and refused to reveal his informant to the grand jury when brought before that body, must go to jail or pay his fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates a legal limit: despite general protections in some states, reporters may be compelled by judicial bodies (e.g., grand juries) to disclose sources and may face criminal penalties for refusal, depending on the case and jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship by injunction unconstitutional (Supreme Court principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Supreme Court decision pointed out that the libel laws afford redress for wrongs committed by publication, but that censorship by injunction is contrary to the Bill of Rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal principle: courts should not impose prior restraints (injunctions) to censor newspapers; libel remedies are provided after publication rather than by prior restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation as a device to limit circulation (constitutional protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: A unanimous decision of the Court held invalid the Louisiana two per cent tax on gross income from advertising in newspapers, calling it 'a deliberate and calculated device in the guise of a tax to limit the circulation of information to which the public is entitled by virtue of the constitutional guarantees.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes that taxes imposed with the effect or intent of limiting circulation/press freedom can be struck down as unconstitutional; protects press against disguised economic censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel law and public discussion of government (Illinois Supreme Court principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Illinois Supreme Court held that a city could not sue for damages by libel, and further declared that 'the people have the right to discuss their government without fear of being called to account in the courts for their expressions of opinion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal standard protecting public discussion/criticism of government from municipal libel suits; emphasizes civic right to debate government without judicial intimidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for journalism education and institutional membership (A.A.S.D.J.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The American Association of Schools and Departments of Journalism, organized in 1917, set up certain standards for institutional membership and acted as a recognizing agency. The A.A.S.D.J. veered from an early emphasis on special journalistic techniques to general acceptance of a curriculum providing a thorough liberal arts background for the special professional courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines institutional evaluation criteria (Class A rating) and curricular recommendation: journalism education should combine thorough liberal arts background with specialized professional courses rather than narrowly technical training alone.
